newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sandoz, Ciba-Geigy stocks dip on merger delay worry.
newsitem.headline: Sandoz, Ciba-Geigy stocks dip on merger delay worry.

text.p: Shares of Swiss pharmaceuticals giants Sandoz AG and Ciba-Geigy AG slipped Monday after a top executive said their mega-merger might be delayed until next year.

Daniel Vasella, designated chief executive officer for the merged Novartis company, said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that a U.S. regulatory review was taking longer than expected.
But securities analysts played down his comments as a worst-case scenario that even if it came true detracted little from the powerful industrial logic behind the merger.

"If I wanted to be very precise, I would say that I am hoping for a January launch of Novartis and when I say hoping it implies that I don't think it completely unrealistic but I also don't think it's a sure bet," Vasella said.

The two firms announced in March a plan to form the second most powerful company in the industry. They got European Union clearance for the deal in July and had originally expected to complete the merger in late summer or early autumn.
News of a possible delay weighed on the companies' shares. In a generally weaker market, Ciba closed 29 Swiss francs ($23.40) lower at 1,555 ($1,254), while Sandoz shed 33 ($26.60) to ($1,169).
Vasella said the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) review of the group's genetic technology operations in the U.S. was taking longer than expected.

"The fact is that we thought that by late fall ... and fall is until Dec. 21, we could get approval. I think it's not impossible but I think the caveat we have to have is this whole area surrounding genetic technology," he said.
"It's a completely new field of activity...It's all research and it's a complex technological area so it takes more time than anticipated to even know if there is any issue or not."
Birgit Kulhoff, an analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland in Zurich, said his comments should not be overdramatised.

"This is still the worst-case scenario, and there is a good chance that the merger can be accomplished before the end of the year," she said. "Even if the worst case arises, it does not change the case for Novartis very much."
Vasella said the two companies were on target with their integration programme and did not anticipate restructuring cost overruns.
"It went faster than planned and we're really now all waiting on the FTC approval in order to start implementing."
The combined company, Novartis, will be second only to Britain's Glaxo Wellcome in pharmaceuticals with a 4.4 percent global market share.
It will have a market capitalisation of some 75 billion Swiss francs ($60.50 billion) and annual sales after spinoffs and divestitures of about 26 billion.
Called the world's biggest corporate merger, the deal dwarfs previous mega-mergers like Walt Disney's acquisition in 1995 of the Capital Cities/ABC television network in the United States.
